title: How orbit speed works
short: Gravity bends a moving spacecraft into an orbit.
body: A spacecraft in a circular orbit keeps falling around the world. Gravity supplies its inward acceleration; it is not cancelled by an outward force in an inertial frame. This equation assumes a spherical central body and a circular orbit.
symbols: v: speed (m/s); G: gravitational constant; M: mass of the central body (kg); r: distance from its centre (m), not altitude.
caption: Your EM0508 Topic 1 slides, page 13 · Singapore Polytechnic / Wall-Pie, 2024.
source: NASA Basics of Space Flight; supplied EM0508 slides

title: Why distant orbits take longer
short: A wider orbit usually takes longer to complete.
body: For two objects orbiting the same much heavier body, the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. An ellipse and a circle with the same semi-major axis have the same period in the two-body model.
symbols: T: period (s); a: semi-major axis (m); G: gravitational constant; M: mass of the central body (kg).
caption: Your EM0508 Topic 4 slides, page 6 · Singapore Polytechnic / Wall-Pie, 2024.
source: NASA Basics of Space Flight; supplied EM0508 slides

title: How a rocket pushes
short: A rocket throws gas one way to move the other way.
body: A rocket carries its propellants. The nozzle speeds up the hot gas as it leaves. Rockets work in a vacuum; they do not need air to push against. The pressure term depends on the pressure outside the nozzle.
symbols: F: thrust (N); ṁ: mass flow (kg/s); vₑ: exhaust speed (m/s); pₑ and pₐ: exit and ambient pressures (Pa); Aₑ: exit area (m²).
caption: Your EM0508 Topic 6 slides, page 4 · Singapore Polytechnic / Wall-Pie, 2024.

title: Gravity on the Moon
short: You weigh about one sixth as much on the Moon.
body: Surface gravity is about 1.62 m/s². Your mass stays the same. The game uses lunar gravity for jumps; moving a heavy rover still takes force.
symbols: W: weight (N); m: mass (kg); g: gravity (m/s²). A 60 kg person weighs about 97 N on the Moon.
caption: An Apollo bootprint in lunar soil · NASA · NASA catalogue date: 2021-04-21

title: No wind on the Moon
short: The Moon has almost no air, so there is no wind.
body: Its extremely thin exosphere cannot carry ordinary wind or sound. Rocket exhaust can kick up dust, which follows ballistic paths rather than billowing like a cloud in air. Music is a soundtrack; suit and cabin sounds are heard through equipment or pressurised air.
caption: The Moon from Orion · NASA · NASA catalogue date: 2026-04-06

title: A very long lunar day
short: Sunrise to sunrise takes about 29.5 Earth days.
body: The Moon rotates in about 27.3 Earth days, but its motion around the Sun makes its solar day about 29.53 Earth days. Near the poles, local terrain changes how long a place stays lit or in shadow. Game time is sped up.

title: Ice in dark polar places
short: Some deep polar shadows can hold water ice.
body: Scientists have detected water ice in permanently shadowed regions near the lunar poles. It is not an everywhere-ready water supply. Finding, digging and processing useful deposits remain engineering challenges.
caption: Lunar polar water-ice observations · NASA · 2017-12-08

title: Artemis I and II: around the Moon
short: Artemis I and II did not land on the Moon.
body: Artemis I tested SLS and Orion without a crew in 2022, including lunar orbit and return to Earth. Artemis II carried four astronauts on a lunar flyby in April 2026. Orion carries crew through deep space and returns them to Earth. The surface game is a separate future-training scenario.
caption: Earth setting behind the Moon, seen from Orion · NASA · NASA catalogue date: 2026-04-06

title: Why the Moon lander looks different
short: A lunar lander needs engines, not a parachute.
body: SLS launches Orion from Earth. A Human Landing System is a separate vehicle for travelling between lunar orbit and the surface. An HLS-inspired Starship has no need for the atmospheric reentry fins and Earth-return heat shield shown on a Mars/Earth Starship concept. Exact designs can change. Our model illustrates the role; it is not a flight-certified blueprint.

title: Real science and game rules
short: Real facts guide the game; distances and time are shortened.
body: Planet facts and images have sources. Terrain is a training landscape, not a surveyed landing site. Resource yields, mission lengths, construction recipes, radiation effects and spacecraft animations are simplified. NASA API keys provide access to particular services; they do not generate models or make every image live.

title: The map-sized world limit
short: Detailed terrain follows the area shown by your minimap.
body: The minimap spans 240 game metres. Map-sized detail loads the tiles touching a 120 m radius around you. Tiles use a small boundary margin so their edges do not expose gaps. A coarse horizon remains beyond it. Your mission state and buildings are not deleted when terrain unloads.
source: Game design; not a NASA measurement

title: Jumping and sprinting on the Moon
short: Less gravity means a longer, higher jump.
body: The game keeps lunar gravity at 1.62 m/s². Walking is 2 m/s; hold Shift to sprint at 4 m/s. The tuned jump launch speed is 2.9 m/s, giving about 2.6 m of rise and 3.6 seconds in the air on level ground. These speeds are game choices, not astronaut performance measurements. A bulky pressurized suit, equipment and technique affect real jumps. With the same launch speed, a lunar jump is about six times higher than on Earth.
symbols: h: rise above takeoff (m); v₀: upward launch speed (m/s); g: gravity (m/s²); t: time back to the same height (s). Ignores air resistance; assumes level landing.
source: NASA reduced-gravity locomotion research; game movement settings

title: NASA Moon and spacecraft models
short: Our flyby Moon uses NASA LRO imagery and topography.
body: On computers and tablets the flyby loads NASA’s original topographic GLB and 8192 × 4096 texture unchanged. Phones automatically load a separate Lite derivative; choose Full quality in Settings to load the original on a phone too. The Orion crew capsule uses NASA’s detailed STL; its service module and arrays are illustrative game geometry. The surface lander is an HLS-inspired training design. NASA’s astronaut and Space Exploration Vehicle models are also used. The walkable terrain is procedural with a NASA LOLA-derived distant horizon; it is not an exact survey of a landing site. Assets load once and are reused; nearby terrain uses bounded chunks.
source: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / LRO; NASA 3D Resources

title: Find the original NASA data
short: NASA’s catalogue helps you find mission datasets.
body: NASA Open Data is a catalogue: it describes datasets and links to the archives that hold them. A catalogue entry is not itself a live measurement. Check the mission, instrument, observation date and units before comparing the data with the game.

title: Earthdata: compare our home planet
short: Earthdata helps us study Earth, not measure Mars weather.
body: Earthdata Search helps you discover Earth-observation datasets. These are useful for comparisons with our home planet, such as ice, land temperature and atmosphere. They are not Mars or Moon surface measurements. Some downloads require an Earthdata Login, separate from a NASA API key.

title: NASA APIs and archived observations
short: An API delivers data; it does not automatically make a scene realistic.
body: NASA APIs provide access to services such as space-weather records. Service availability varies: NASA listed the older Mars Rover Photos API as archived when checked on 8 November 2026. The game has separate rover-image and Earth-image loaders with archived fallbacks. Its private API key is used only by an offline data-fetch script, never shipped in the browser. A solar event record is not a direct measurement of radiation at your outpost.

title: How scientists map Mars heights
short: Laser measurements let scientists build maps of Mars heights.
body: The terrain now samples NASA MOLA MEGDR product MEGT00N090HB.IMG: 512 × 512 native signed elevation samples around Gusev Crater, at 128 pixels per degree (about 463 metres between north-south samples). This is archived altimetry, including interpolated bins supplied by NASA, not new live observations. A 4-degree region (about 230 × 237 km) is compressed into a 640 × 640 game-metre map. Height differences are multiplied by 0.015, giving roughly 5.5 times vertical exaggeration relative to the horizontal compression. The central 70 game metres are flattened and blend into the measurements by radius 115 metres. Procedural hills have been removed; rocks and sand are decorative. Every landing scenario currently shares this Gusev training terrain. Source product dates to March 2003; downloaded 8 November 2026.

title: NASA Open APIs
short: Use the portal to discover individual services and their authentication requirements. Prefer the existing imagery connections for mission briefings.
body: Use the portal to discover individual services and their authentication requirements. Prefer the existing imagery connections for mission briefings. This is a directory, not one gameplay dataset. Keep keys out of browser code; cache selected records.

title: DONKI space weather
short: Use historical flare and solar-particle events as dated storm-story prompts.
body: Use historical flare and solar-particle events as dated storm-story prompts. Research-quality events are not a guaranteed Mars forecast. A flare class alone does not determine surface radiation. Official host migrated in September 2026.

title: OSDR space biology
short: Use selected plant and microbial studies as evidence cards: organism, flight conditions, controls, study accession and original publication. OSD-37 provides a plant comparison.
body: Use selected plant and microbial studies as evidence cards: organism, flight conditions, controls, study accession and original publication. OSD-37 provides a plant comparison. Earth organisms studied in space are not Martian life. Metadata alone does not establish effect size, causation or crop yields.

title: RadLab radiation instruments
short: Compare readings from a named instrument, location and time interval. Teach why exposure depends on environment and shielding.
body: Compare readings from a named instrument, location and time interval. Teach why exposure depends on environment and shielding. Absorbed dose rate is microgray/hour; dose equivalent rate is microsievert/hour. Do not treat them as interchangeable or copy ISS readings onto Mars.

title: Mars Trek terrain
short: Use mapped imagery for mission-site context; the existing game already uses NASA terrain. Consult WMTS layers for a future site-specific map.
body: Use mapped imagery for mission-site context; the existing game already uses NASA terrain. Consult WMTS layers for a future site-specific map. Image tiles are not elevation grids. Respect layer projection, coverage, resolution and attribution. The current world stays Gusev-based even when another region is selected.

title: CSA youth and STEM resources
short: Use educator activities for debriefs, learning goals and classroom extensions.
body: Use educator activities for debriefs, learning goals and classroom extensions. This is a curated resource directory, not a live API. Link to original activities and check reproduction terms for media.

title: CSA food-production toolkit
short: Use food production challenges to connect crop choices with water, light, nutrition, preparation and waste. Keep packaged food in reserve.
body: Use food production challenges to connect crop choices with water, light, nutrition, preparation and waste. Keep packaged food in reserve. Real crops grow over days or months. Game seconds and simplified food rewards must stay labelled as training rules.

title: Explore NASA space-weather events
short: DONKI records solar flares, coronal mass ejections and other space-weather events.
body: NASA’s DONKI (Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) lets you explore recorded space-weather events and their links to observations. The outpost’s radiation scenario is a simplified training simulation; archived solar events are not a live radiation reading at this base.
source: NASA Community Coordinated Modeling Center — DONKI

title: Explore Mars with Mars Trek
short: Compare the game’s training landscape with NASA Mars maps.
body: Mars Trek is NASA’s web mapping tool for exploring Mars. Use it to see how real orbital imagery and map layers provide context for a landing site. This game’s walkable Gusev landscape is a compressed training area, not a surveyed reconstruction of the terrain shown in Mars Trek.

title: How radiation is measured in space
short: RadLab lets you inspect readings from real spacecraft instruments.
body: NASA RadLab lets you filter radiation records by spacecraft, instrument and time. Some records include absorbed dose rate (μGy/hour), dose equivalent rate (μSv/hour), particle flux and orbit or trajectory details. These are measurements from the listed instrument and location; an ISS reading is not a real-time radiation measurement at this Mars base. The game’s radiation scenario is a simplified simulation.

title: Space biology experiments and datasets
short: NASA OSDR publishes research on plants and life in space.
body: NASA’s Open Science Data Repository collects research datasets from spaceflight and ground studies. Search for plant investigations such as VEG-05 or XROOTS to learn how researchers study crop growth, plant-associated microbes and hydroponic or aeroponic systems. These experiments help scientists ask research questions; they are not a ready-made Mars greenhouse operating manual.

title: Plan food for a remote outpost
short: The Canadian Space Agency has food and nutrition activities for Grades 6–9.
body: The CSA food-production toolkit connects food in space with astronaut health and nutrition. Its activities include Interplanetary Farming, Master Chef: Mars, food safety and reading food labels. Use them to plan a varied menu and discuss which ingredients an outpost can grow, store or recycle. The activities are classroom resources, not mission-certified food-system designs.
source: Canadian Space Agency — Food production toolkit

title: Find more space and STEM activities
short: The Canadian Space Agency shares STEM resources for youth and educators.
body: Browse Canadian Space Agency resources and youth organizations for activities that connect space exploration with science, technology, engineering and mathematics. Use the listings to find age-appropriate classroom and youth-program material; they are learning resources, not mission operating procedures.
source: Canadian Space Agency — STEM and youth resources
